label: cong
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{cong}
Two nonsingular matrices $A$ and $B$ in $PGL(3,\mathbb{F}_q)$  are congruent if and only if their corresponding curves $C_A$ and $C_B$ are projectively equivalent. More precisely, a matrix $T \in GL(3, \mathbb{F}_q)$ satisfies $B = \lambda T^* A T$ for some $\lambda \in \mathbb{F}_q^*$ if and only if $T$ induces a projective transformation from $C_B$ to $C_A$.

label: mirror
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{mirror}
For a mirror pair $(C_A, C_{A^*})$, the following properties hold:
\begin{enumerate}[{\rm (i)}]
\item $C_A(\mathbb{F}_q) = C_{A^*}(\mathbb{F}_q)$.
\item For $P \in C_A(\mathbb{F}_q)$, $P$ is an inflexion of $C_A$ if and only if it is an inflexion of $C_{A^*}$. In this case, their tangent lines coincide, i.e., $\mathcal{L}_P(C_A) = \mathcal{L}_P(C_{A^*})$.
\item If $P \in C_A(\mathbb{F}_q)$ is not an inflexion, there exists a unique point $P' \in C_A(\mathbb{F}_q) \setminus \{P\}$ such that the intersection divisor satisfies $C_A \cdot \mathcal{L}_P(C_A) = \sqrt{q}P + P'$. In this case, the intersection divisor for the mirror curve satisfies $C_{A^*} \cdot \mathcal{L}_{P'}(C_{A^*}) = \sqrt{q}P' + P$. In particular, $P'$ is also a non-inflexion of $C_{A^*}$.
\end{enumerate}

label: mirror-inter
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{mirror-inter}
Let $C_A$ be a Hermitian-relative curve that is not a Hermitian curve. Then the following hold:
\begin{enumerate}[{\rm (i)}]
\item $\sum_{P \in C_A(\mathbb{F}_q)} i(C_A \cdot C_{A^*}; P) \le \sum_{P \in C_A(\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q)} i(C_A \cdot C_{A^*}; P) = (\sqrt{q}+1)^2$.
\item If $P$ is an inflexion of $C_A$, then $i(C_A \cdot C_{A^*}; P) \ge \sqrt{q}+1$.
\item $N_q(C_A) \le (\sqrt{q}+1)^2$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: (i) Since $C_A(\mathbb{F}_q) \subseteq C_A(\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q)$, the inequality follows immediately. The equality is a direct consequence of Bézout's theorem.   (ii) If $P$ is an inflexion of $C_A$, then by Proposition \ref{mirror}, it is also an inflexion of $C_{A^*}$ and their tangent lines at $P$ coincide. Let $\mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_P(C_A) = \mathcal{L}_P(C_{A^*})$. By the characterization of inflexions on these curves, we have $i(C_A \cdot \mathcal{L}; P) = \sqrt{q}+1$ and $i(C_{A^*} \cdot \mathcal{L}; P) = \sqrt{q}+1$. This implies that $i(C_A \cdot C_{A^*}; P) \ge \sqrt{q}+1$. (iii) Since $C_A(\mathbb{F}_q) = C_{A^*}(\mathbb{F}_q)$ by Proposition \ref{mirror}, each $P \in C_A(\mathbb{F}_q)$ contributes at least $1$ to the intersection multiplicity $i(C_A \cdot C_{A^*}; P)$. Therefore, $N_q(C_A) \le \sum_{P \in C_A(\mathbb{F}_q)} i(C_A \cdot C_{A^*}; P)$, which is at most $(\sqrt{q}+1)^2$ by (1).

\label{degsqrtq}
Let $\alpha \in \mathbb{F}_q^{\ast}$ and $\beta \in \mathbb{F}_q$,
and consider the equation in $X$:

 \item When $\mathrm{Nm} (\alpha) =1$, 
$(\ref{sq10})$ has a solution in $\mathbb{F}_q$ if and only if
$\beta =0$ or $\alpha = \beta^{1-\sqrt{q}}$ (which is equivalent to $\alpha^{\sqrt{q}}=\beta^{\sqrt{q}-1}$).
In this case, \eqref{sq10} possesses $\sqrt{q}$ distinct roots, all of which are $\mathbb{F}_q$-solutions.
                                                           
 \item If $\mathrm{Nm}( \alpha) \neq 1$, then $(\ref{sq10})$
 has a unique $\mathbb{F}_q$-solution.
 \item
 In particular, when $\alpha=-1$, \eqref{sq10} has a solution if and only if $\mathrm{Tr}(\beta) =0$.
\end{enumerate}

label: ext_varphi
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{ext_varphi}
Let $A \in GL(3, \mathbb{F}_q)$. For any point $P \in C_A$, not necessarily an $\mathbb{F}_q$-rational point, there exists a unique point $P' \in C_A$ such that $\mathcal{L}_P C_A \cdot C_A = \sqrt{q}P + P'$. The map $\varphi_A : C_A \to C_A$, defined by $\varphi_A(P) = P'$, can be expressed explicitly as 
\[
\varphi_A(P) = A^{-1}A^* P^{(q)},
\]
where $((x, y, z)^t)^{(q)} = (x^q, y^q, z^q)^t$. Note that if $P$ is an $\mathbb{F}_q$-rational point, then $P^{(q)} = P$, so this expression is consistent with the definition of $\varphi$ in Proposition~\ref{mirror}.
head: environment

label: varphiAP
title: Proof
body_md:
Let $C_J$ be the Hermitian curve defined by $x^{\sqrt{q}+1} + y^{\sqrt{q}}z + yz^{\sqrt{q}} = 0$, which corresponds to the matrix $J = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$. Since $J = J^*$, the curve $C_J$ is Hermitian. Since $C_J$ and $C_A$ are projectively equivalent over $\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q$~\cite{par1986}, there exists a matrix $T \in GL(3, \overline{\mathbb{F}}_q)$ such that $T^* J T = A$. It is well known that the map $\varphi_J$ for $C_J$ is given by $\varphi_J(P) = P^{(q)}$ (see, e.g., \cite[Lemma 3.1]{hom2006}). Since the projective transformation $T$ induces an isomorphism between $C_A$ and $C_J$ while preserving tangency, the map $\varphi_A$ can be expressed via conjugation as:
\begin{equation}\label{varphiAP}
\varphi_A(P) = T^{-1} \varphi_J(T P) = T^{-1} (T P)^{(q)} = T^{-1} T^{(q)} P^{(q)}.
\end{equation}
The relation $T^* J T = A$ implies $T^{-1} = A^{-1} T^* J$. Taking the Hermitian adjoint of $A = T^* J T$ yields $A^* = T^* J T^{(q)}$, or equivalently $T^{(q)} = J (T^*)^{-1} A^*$. Given $J^2 = I$, their product simplifies directly to:

$$T^{-1} T^{(q)} = (A^{-1} T^* J)(J (T^*)^{-1} A^*) = A^{-1} A^*.$$
Thus, we obtain the explicit expression $\varphi_A(P) = A^{-1} A^* P^{(q)}$.

body_md: \label{eigenvector} Let $A \in GL(3, \mathbb{F}_{q})$ and $P \in C_A(\mathbb{F}_{q})$. Then $P$ is an inflexion of $C_A$ if and only if $P$ is an eigenvector of the matrix $A^{-1}A^*$.

title: Proof
body_md: By the definition of the map $\varphi_A$, a point $P$ is an inflexion if and only if $\varphi_A(P) = P$ in $\mathbb{P}^2$. For $P \in C_A( \mathbb{F}_q)$, we have $P^{(q)} = P$, and thus the condition $\varphi_A(P) = P$ is equivalent to $A^{-1}A^* P = \lambda P$ for some $\lambda \in \mathbb{F}_q^*$. This is precisely the condition that $P$ is an eigenvector of $A^{-1}A^*$, which completes the proof.

title: Proof
body_md:
Note that the points $(1,0,0)^t$, $(0,1,0)^t$, and $(0,0,1)^t$ lie on $C_{a,b}$. At the point $P=(1,0,0)^t$, the tangent line $\mathcal{L}_P$ meets the curve at $(0,1,0)^t$ as well. This implies that the intersection multiplicity of $\mathcal{L}_PC_{a,b}$ and $C$ at $P$ is less than the order required for an inflexion, confirming that $P$ is a non-inflexion point.

Conversely, suppose that a Hermitian-relative curve $C$ possesses an $\mathbb{F}_q$-rational point $P$ that is not an inflexion. The fact that $P$ is not an inflexion implies $\varphi(P) \neq P$. From the intersection relations $\mathcal{L}_P C \cdot C = \sqrt{q}P + \varphi(P)$ and $\mathcal{L}_{\varphi(P)} C \cdot C = \sqrt{q}\varphi(P) + \varphi^2(P)$, it follows that the two tangent lines $\mathcal{L}_P C$ and $\mathcal{L}_{\varphi(P)} C$ are distinct and intersect at the point $\varphi(P)$. Consequently, the three points $P$, $\varphi(P)$, and $\varphi^2(P)$ are not collinear.  Since the three points $P, \varphi(P)$, and $\varphi^2(P)$ are not collinear, we may assume, without loss of generality, that $P = (1, 0, 0)^t$, $\varphi(P) = (0, 1, 0)^t$, and $\varphi^2(P) = (0, 0, 1)^t$ by applying a suitable projective transformation. 
Let $A = (a_{ij}) \in GL(3, \mathbb{F}_q)$ be the matrix corresponding to $C$; that is, $C = C_A$. Since the tangent line $\mathcal{L}_P C$ passes through both $P = (1, 0, 0)^t$ and $\varphi(P) = (0, 1, 0)^t$, its equation is given by $z = 0$. Similarly, $\mathcal{L}_{\varphi(P)} C$ passes through $\varphi(P) = (0, 1, 0)^t$ and $\varphi^2(P) = (0, 0, 1)^t$, and hence its equation is $x = 0$. On the other hand, the coefficients of the tangent lines $\mathcal{L}_P C$ and $\mathcal{L}_{\varphi(P)} C$ are given by $[a_{11}, a_{12}, a_{13}]$ and $[a_{21}, a_{22}, a_{23}]$, respectively. Comparing these with the equations $z = 0$ and $x = 0$, we obtain$$a_{11} = a_{12} = a_{22} = a_{23} = 0.$$ Furthermore, since the curve $C_A$ passes through $(0, 0, 1)^t$, it follows that $a_{33} = 0$. Since $A$ is non-singular, the entry $a_{13}$ must be non-zero (otherwise, the first row would be zero). Thus, we may divide the matrix by $a_{13}$ and assume, without loss of generality, that $a_{13} = 1$. Consequently, the matrix $A$ takes the form
$$A = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & 1 \\ a_{21} & 0 & 0 \\ a_{31} & a_{32} & 0 \end{pmatrix}.$$
Since the determinant of $A$, given by $-a_{21} a_{32}$, is non-zero, it follows that $a_{21} \neq 0$ and $a_{32} \neq 0$. The corresponding equation for the curve is then
$$ x^{\sqrt{q}} z + a_{21} x y^{\sqrt{q}} + a_{31} x z^{\sqrt{q}} + a_{32} y z^{\sqrt{q}} = 0.$$
If we let $T = \text{diag}(1, a_{21}^{-\sqrt{q}}, 1)$, then 
\[
T^*AT = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ a_{31} & a_{32} a_{21}^{-\sqrt{q}} & 0 \end{pmatrix}.
\]
Upon substituting $b = a_{31}$ and $a = a_{32} a_{21}^{-\sqrt{q}}$, the matrix $A$ is transformed into the canonical form associated with the curve $C_{a,b}$:
\[
\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ b & a & 0 \end{pmatrix}.
\]
Note that $a \neq 0$ since $a_{21}$ and $a_{32}$ are non-zero.

body_md:
\label{I_qCa0}
The number $I_q(C_{a,0})$ of rational inflexions of the curve $C_{a,0}$ is determined by the value of $\sqrt{q}$ modulo $3$ as follows:
\begin{enumerate}[{\rm (i)}]
\item If $\sqrt{q} \equiv 0 \pmod{3}$, then $I_q(C_{a,0}) = 1$.
\item If $\sqrt{q} \equiv 1 \pmod{3}$, then $I_q(C_{a,0}) = 2$.
\item If $\sqrt{q} \equiv 2 \pmod{3}$, then $I_q(C_{a,0}) = 0$.
\end{enumerate}

label: charpoly
title: Proof
body_md:
Since the two points $(1, 0, 0)^t$ and $(0, 1, 0)^t$ on the line at infinity $z=0$ are not inflexions, it suffices to search for inflexions within the affine plane $z \neq 0$.

The matrix associated with the curve $C_{a,0}$ is given by
$$A = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & a & 0 \end{pmatrix}.$$
To apply Proposition~\ref{eigenvector}, we consider the matrix $U = A^{-1} A^*$.  A straightforward calculation yields
$$U = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & a^{\sqrt{q}} \\ 1/a & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix},$$
and its characteristic polynomial is
\begin{equation}\label{charpoly}
P_U(\lambda) = \det(\lambda I - U) = \lambda^3 - a^{\sqrt{q}-1}.
\end{equation}
For an eigenvalue $\lambda$ of $U$,   a straightforward calculation shows that the coordinates of the eigenvector satisfy
$$(x_0, y_0, 1)^t = \left( \frac{a^{\sqrt{q}}}{\lambda}, \lambda, 1 \right)^t.$$
Substituting these coordinates into the left-hand side of the affine equation \eqref{Ca0aff}, and utilizing the relation $\lambda^3 = a^{\sqrt{q}-1}$, the expression simplifies as follows:
\begin{equation}\label{Ca0lambda}
x_0^{\sqrt{q}} + x_0 y_0^{\sqrt{q}} + a y_0 = \frac{a}{\lambda^{\sqrt{q}}} \left( \lambda^{2(\sqrt{q}+1)} + \lambda^{\sqrt{q}+1} + 1 \right). 
\end{equation}
According to Proposition~\ref{eigenvector}, a point $(x_0, y_0, 1)^t$ on the curve is an inflexion if and only if it is an eigenvector of $U = A^{-1} A^*$. 
 
Hence the expression in \eqref{Ca0lambda} must vanish. Since $a / \lambda^{\sqrt{q}} \neq 0$ in \eqref{Ca0lambda}, we can divide by this factor to obtain the second equation in the system below. Consequently, the number of rational inflexions is equal to the number of solutions for $\lambda$ in the following system:
\begin{equation}\label{eqinfl}
\begin{cases}\lambda^3 - a^{\sqrt{q}-1} = 0, \\\lambda^{2(\sqrt{q}+1)} + \lambda^{\sqrt{q}+1} + 1 = 0.\end{cases}\end{equation}
(i) The case $\sqrt{q} \equiv 0 \pmod{3}$. In this case, the characteristic of $\mathbb{F}_q$ is $3$. Since the Frobenius map $\sigma: u \mapsto u^3$ is an automorphism of $\mathbb{F}_q$, the equation $\lambda^3 = a^{\sqrt{q}-1}$ has a unique solution in $\mathbb{F}_q$, given by $\lambda = (a^{\sqrt{q}-1})^{q/3}$. Substituting this into the second equation of \eqref{eqinfl}, we obtain:
\begin{equation*}
\left( a^{\frac{q(\sqrt{q}-1)}{3}} \right)^{2(\sqrt{q}+1)} + \left( a^{\frac{q(\sqrt{q}-1)}{3}} \right)^{\sqrt{q}+1} + 1 =  a^{(q-1)\frac{2q }{3}}  +  a^{(q-1)\frac{q }{3}}  + 1 =  0.
\end{equation*}
Therefore, the system \eqref{eqinfl} has a unique solution for $\lambda$, which implies that the curve has a unique rational inflexion.

\noindent (ii) The case $\sqrt{q} \equiv 1 \pmod{3}$. In this case, $3$ divides $\sqrt{q}-1$, consequently, 3 also divides $q-1$. The equation $\lambda^3 = a^{\sqrt{q}-1} $ possesses three distinct roots in $\mathbb{F}_q$, given by:
\begin{equation}\label{3sol} a^{\frac{  \sqrt{q}-1 }{3}}, \quad \zeta  a^{\frac{  \sqrt{q}-1 }{3}}, \quad \zeta^2  a^{\frac{  \sqrt{q}-1 }{3}},
\end{equation}
where $\zeta$ is a primitive cube root of unity (i.e., a root of $X^3=1$). Since $3 \mid (\sqrt{q}-1)$, it follows that $\zeta$ lies in the subfield $\mathbb{F}_{\sqrt{q}}^* \subset \mathbb{F}_q^*$. 

Let $\rho = \mathrm{Nm}\left( a^{\frac{\sqrt{q}-1}{3}} \right)$. Note that $\rho = a^{\frac{q-1}{3}}$, which implies $\rho^3 = 1$. Then the norms of the other two roots are given by:$$\mathrm{Nm}\left( \zeta a^{\frac{\sqrt{q}-1}{3}} \right) = \zeta^{\sqrt{q}+1} \rho = \zeta^2 \rho, \quad \text{and} \quad
\mathrm{Nm}\left( \zeta^2 a^{\frac{\sqrt{q}-1}{3}} \right) = \zeta^{2(\sqrt{q}+1)} \rho = \zeta \rho.$$

Thus, the set of norms of the three roots, $\{\rho, \zeta^2 \rho, \zeta \rho\}$, consists of distinct cube roots of unity, and is therefore a permutation of $\{1, \zeta, \zeta^2\}$. On the other hand, the left-hand side of the second equation in \eqref{eqinfl} can be written as $\mathrm{Nm}(\lambda)^2 + \mathrm{Nm}(\lambda) + 1$.  Among the three possible values for the norm, $\zeta$ and $\zeta^2$ satisfy this equation, whereas $1$ does not (since the characteristic is not $3$). Consequently, there are exactly two solutions for $\lambda$, which implies that the curve has exactly two rational inflexions.

\noindent (iii) The case $\sqrt{q} \equiv 2 \pmod{3}$. In this case, we have $3 \mid (\sqrt{q}+1)$, which implies $\gcd(3, \sqrt{q}-1) = 1$. Suppose that $\lambda_0$ be a solution to the equation $\lambda_0^3 = a^{\sqrt{q}-1}$ in $\mathbb{F}_q$. To determine the norm of this solution, we observe that:$$\left( \mathrm{Nm}(\lambda_0) \right)^3 = (\lambda_0^3)^{\sqrt{q}+1} = (a^{\sqrt{q}-1})^{\sqrt{q}+1} = a^{q-1} = 1.$$Since $\gcd(3, \sqrt{q}-1) = 1$, the only cube root of unity in the subfield $\mathbb{F}_{\sqrt{q}}$ is $1$ itself. Therefore, it follows that:
$$\mathrm{Nm}(\lambda_0) = \lambda_0^{\sqrt{q}+1} = 1.$$
Substituting this into the left-hand side of the second equation in \eqref{eqinfl}, we obtain:
$$\lambda_0^{2(\sqrt{q}+1)} + \lambda_0^{\sqrt{q}+1} + 1 = 1^2 + 1 + 1 = 3 \neq 0,$$
as the characteristic of the field is not $3$. Consequently, there are no solutions to \eqref{eqinfl} for $\lambda_0$ in this case, meaning that the curve has no rational inflexions.

title: Proof
body_md:
Note that $A_{a,b} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ b & a & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ is the matrix corresponding to $C_{a,b}$. Let $T$ be the diagonal matrix $T = \mathrm{diag}(ba^{\sqrt{q}}, -b^{\sqrt{q}}, 1)$. A direct calculation yields
$$T^* A_{a,b} T = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & ab^{\sqrt{q}} \\ -b^2a^{\sqrt{q}} & 0 & 0 \\ b^2a^{\sqrt{q}} & -ab^{\sqrt{q}} & 0 \end{pmatrix} = ab^{\sqrt{q}} \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & 1 \\ -c & 0 & 0 \\ c & -1 & 0 
\end{pmatrix},$$
where $c = \frac{b^2 a^{\sqrt{q}}}{a b^{\sqrt{q}}} = b (\frac{a}{b})^{\sqrt{q}-1}$. Since $ab^{\sqrt{q}}$ is a non-zero scalar, this matrix is equivalent to $M_c$ in $PGL(3, \mathbb{F}_q)$, which proves the projective equivalence of $C_{a,b}$ and $C_c$. Conversely, for any $c \in \mathbb{F}_q^*$, we can choose $a = b = c$. In this case, the parameter $c$ in our transformation becomes $c (\frac{c}{c})^{\sqrt{q}-1} = c$. Thus, $C_{c,c}$ is projectively equivalent to $C_c$, showing that every $C_c$ can be realized as a curve of the form $C_{a,b}$.

label: mathcalY
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{mathcalY} For the curve $C_c$, the following properties hold:
\begin{enumerate}[{\rm(i)}]
\item $|\mathcal{Y}_1| = \sqrt{q} + 1$ and $|\mathcal{Y}_0| =q-( \sqrt{q} + 1)$.
\item For each $y_0 \in \mathcal{Y}_0$, the line $y = y_0$ intersects $C_c^\circ$ at exactly one $\mathbb{F}_q$-point.
\item\label{sqline} For each $y_0 \in \mathcal{Y}_1$, the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[{\rm(a)}]
\item The line $y = y_0$ intersects the affine curve $C_c^\circ$ at an $\mathbb{F}_q$-point.
\item The line $y = y_0$ is a $\mathbb{F}_q$-rational $\sqrt{q}$-line of $C_c^\circ$; that is, $|(y = y_0) \cap C_c^\circ(\mathbb{F}_q)| = \sqrt{q}$.
\item $y_0 = 0$ or $y_0^{1-\sqrt{q}} = -c(y_0^{\sqrt{q}} - 1)$.
\item $y_0 = 0$ or $y_0^{\sqrt{q}-1} +c^{\sqrt{q}} y_0  - c^{\sqrt{q}}=0$.
\end{enumerate}
\item\label{ssqrtq} Let $s$ be the number of points in $\mathcal{Y}_1$ that satisfy the equivalent conditions in item \ref{sqline}. Then, the total number of $\mathbb{F}_q$-rational points on $C_c$ is given by
$$N_q(C_c) = (q - \sqrt{q} + 1) + s\sqrt{q}.$$
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
(i) Since the map $y \mapsto c(y^{\sqrt{q}}-1)$ is a bijection on $\mathbb{F}_q$ and $|\ker(\mathrm{Nm})| = \sqrt{q} + 1$, it follows that $|\mathcal{Y}_1| = \sqrt{q} + 1$, and consequently $|\mathcal{Y}_0| = q - \sqrt{q} - 1$.
(ii) If $y_0 \in \mathcal{Y}_0$, then $\mathrm{Nm}(-c(y_0^{\sqrt{q}}-1)) = \mathrm{Nm}(c(y_0^{\sqrt{q}}-1)) \neq 1$. According to Proposition \ref{degsqrtq}, it follows that equation \eqref{eq:affCc} possesses exactly one solution as an equation in $x$. This implies that the line $y = y_0$ intersects $C_c^\circ$ at precisely one point.
(iii) For $y_0 \in \mathcal{Y}_1$, Proposition \ref{degsqrtq} implies that the equation has $\sqrt{q}$ distinct roots if and only if $y_0 = 0$ or $y_0^{1-\sqrt{q}} = -c(y_0^{\sqrt{q}} - 1)$. Equivalently, this condition can be written as $y_0 = 0$ or $y_0^{\sqrt{q}-1} = -c^{\sqrt{q}}(y_0 - 1)$. If neither condition is satisfied, the equation possesses no roots.
(iv) There are two $\mathbb{F}_q$-points on the line $z = 0$. The affine plane where $z \neq 0$ can be expressed as a disjoint union of $q$ lines of the form $y = y_0$ for $y_0 \in \mathbb{F}_q$. Among these, for the $q - \sqrt{q} - 1$ values of $y_0$ belonging to $\mathcal{Y}_0$, each corresponding line contains exactly one $\mathbb{F}_q$-point. Combining these with the two points at infinity, we obtain $q - \sqrt{q} + 1$ points. Furthermore, for $y_0 \in \mathcal{Y}_1$, we have defined $s$ as the number of such points satisfying the conditions in item (3). Since each of these $s$ lines contributes $\sqrt{q}$ points, an additional $s\sqrt{q}$ points are added to the total.

title: Corollary
body_md: Every Hermitian-relative curve possessing at least one $\mathbb{F}_q$-point that is not an inflexion has at least $q - \sqrt{q} + 1$ $\mathbb{F}_q$-rational points.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: A Hermitian-relative curve $C$ possessing at least one $\mathbb{F}_q$-point that is not an inflexion is projectively equivalent to the curve $C_{a,b}$ defined by \eqref{eqCab}. In the case where $b=0$, it follows from Proposition \ref{N_qCa0} that $N_q(C_{a,0}) \ge q - \sqrt{q} + 1$. When $b \neq 0$, the curve is projectively equivalent to $C_c$ defined by \eqref{eq:Cc} according to Proposition \ref{prop:Cc}. Consequently, Lemma \ref{mathcalY} \ref{ssqrtq} implies that $N_q(C_c) \ge q - \sqrt{q} + 1$, which completes the proof.

title: Proof
body_md:
(i) If $(x_0 , y_0 , 1)^t $ is an inflexion, then it is an eigenvector of $U$ by Proposition \ref{eigenvector}. If $\lambda_0$ is the corresponding eigenvalue to it, we have \eqref{matrixeq}. From \eqref{systeq} we have $\lambda_0 = \frac{1}{cx_0}$. 

(ii) If the line $y=y_0$ is a $\sqrt{q}$-line of $C_c^\circ$, then Lemma \ref{mathcalY} implies that $y_0 \in \mathcal{Y}_1$ and that either $y_0=0$ or $y_0^{1-\sqrt{q}}=-c(y_0^{\sqrt{q}}-1)$ holds.
In the case $y_0 = 0$, the condition $y_0 \in \mathcal{Y}_1$ implies $\mathrm{Nm}(c) = \mathrm{Nm}(-c) = 1$. Consequently, we have:
$$P_U(c^{\sqrt{q}}(1-y_0)) = P_U(c^{\sqrt{q}}) = (c^{\sqrt{q}})^3 - c^{\sqrt{q}}(c^{\sqrt{q}})^2 + c^{\sqrt{q}}(c^{\sqrt{q}}) - c^{\sqrt{q}-1} = 0,$$
since $c^{\sqrt{q}+1} = \mathrm{Nm}(c) = 1$ implies $c^{\sqrt{q}} = c^{-1}$.
In the case where $y_0^{1-\sqrt{q}} = -c(y_0^{\sqrt{q}} - 1)$, raising both sides to the $\sqrt{q}$-th power yields $y_0^{\sqrt{q}-1} = -c^{\sqrt{q}}(y_0 - 1)$. 
                                                                           
Hence we obtain:
$$\begin{aligned}
P_U(c^{\sqrt{q} }(1-y_0 ))  = P_U(y_0^{\sqrt{q}-1}) &= (y_0^{\sqrt{q}-1})^3 - c^{\sqrt{q}} (y_0^{\sqrt{q}-1})^2 + c^{\sqrt{q}} (y_0^{\sqrt{q}-1}) - c^{\sqrt{q}-1} \\
&= (y_0^{\sqrt{q}-1} - c^{\sqrt{q}}) (y_0^{\sqrt{q}-1})^2 + c^{\sqrt{q}} (y_0^{\sqrt{q}-1}) - c^{\sqrt{q}-1}\\
&= (-c^{\sqrt{q}}y_0) (y_0^{\sqrt{q}-1})^2 + c^{\sqrt{q}} (y_0^{\sqrt{q}-1}) - c^{\sqrt{q}-1} \\
&= -c^{\sqrt{q}} y_0^{2\sqrt{q}-1} + c^{\sqrt{q}} y_0^{\sqrt{q}-1} - c^{\sqrt{q}-1} \\
&= c^{\sqrt{q}} y_0^{\sqrt{q}-1} (-y_0^{\sqrt{q}} + 1) - c^{\sqrt{q}-1} \\
&= c^{\sqrt{q}-1}  (y_0^{\sqrt{q}-1}) (-c(y_0^{\sqrt{q}} - 1)) - c^{\sqrt{q}-1} \\
&= c^{\sqrt{q}-1} (y_0^{\sqrt{q}-1} \cdot y_0^{1-\sqrt{q}}) - c^{\sqrt{q}-1} = 0.
\end{aligned}$$
Thus  $c^{\sqrt{q} }(1-y_0 )$ is a root of $P_U (\lambda)$.
Finally, since $y_0 \in \mathcal{Y}_1$, we have $\mathrm{Nm}(c(y_0^{\sqrt{q}}-1)) = 1$. This implies that the element $c^{\sqrt{q}}(1-y_0)$ is also a $(\sqrt{q}+1)$-th root of unity, as its norm satisfies:
$$\mathrm{Nm}(c^{\sqrt{q}}(1-y_0)) =\mathrm{Nm}(c(y_0^{\sqrt{q}}-1)) = 1.$$

(ii) Note that the eigenvalues of $U^*$ are the $\sqrt{q}$-th powers of those of $U$, while the eigenvalues of $U^{-1}$ are the reciprocals of the eigenvalues of $U$. 
Let $\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \lambda_3 \in \overline{\mathbb{F}}_q$ be the eigenvalues of $U$, counted with multiplicity. Then the eigenvalues of $U^*$ and $U^{-1}$ are given by $\lambda_1^{\sqrt{q}}, \lambda_2^{\sqrt{q}}, \lambda_3^{\sqrt{q}}$ and $\lambda_1^{-1}, \lambda_2^{-1}, \lambda_3^{-1}$, respectively. These two sequences of eigenvalues are identical up to reordering by   (i), which leads to (ii).

label: 5polys
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{5polys}
For each $c \in \mathbb{F}_q^*$, the polynomial $P_{U_c}(\lambda)$ either splits completely into linear factors over $\mathbb{F}_q$ or is irreducible over $\mathbb{F}_q$. More precisely, exactly one of the following holds:
\begin{enumerate}[\rm(i)]
\item $P_{U_c}(\lambda)$ has a triple root. This occurs only when $\lambda=1$,  $c=3$ and $p \neq 3$.
\item $P_{U_c}(\lambda)$ has a double root and a simple root, both of which are $(\sqrt{q}+1)$-th roots of unity.
\item $P_{U_c}(\lambda)$ has three distinct simple roots, all of which are $(\sqrt{q}+1)$-th roots of unity.
\item $P_{U_c}(\lambda)$ has three distinct simple roots, only one of which is a $(\sqrt{q}+1)$-th root of unity, while the other two, say $\beta$ and $\gamma$, satisfy $\beta^{\sqrt{q}} = \gamma^{-1}$.
\item $P_{U_c}(\lambda)$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{F}_q$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
As in the lemma above, let $\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \lambda_3 \in \overline{\mathbb{F}}_q$ be  the eigenvalues of $U_c$, counted with multiplicity. We first classify the cases based on whether $P_{U_c}(\lambda)$ has a triple root, a double root, or three distinct roots. 

{\bf Case 1:} $P_{U_c}(\lambda)$ has a triple root. In this case, we have $\lambda_1 = \lambda_2 = \lambda_3$. From the relation $\{\lambda_i^{\sqrt{q}}\} = \{\lambda_i^{-1}\}$, it follows that $\lambda_1^{\sqrt{q}+1} = 1$, which implies $\lambda_1 \in \mathbb{F}_q$. The characteristic polynomial is then expressed as:
$$P_{U_c}(\lambda) = (\lambda - \lambda_1)^3 = \lambda^3 - 3\lambda_1\lambda^2 + 3\lambda_1^2\lambda - \lambda_1^3.$$
By comparing these coefficients with $P_{U_c}(\lambda) = \lambda^3 - c^{\sqrt{q}} \lambda^2 +  c^{\sqrt{q}} \lambda - c^{\sqrt{q}-1}$ and recalling $c\ne 0$ and $\lambda_1 \ne 0$, we know that $\lambda_1=1$, $c=3$ and $p\ne 3$.
 


{\bf Case 2:}  Suppose $P_{U_c}(\lambda)$ has a double root and a simple root, and let $\lambda_1 = \lambda_2 \ne \lambda_3$. Since the operation of taking $\sqrt{q}$-th powers and reciprocals preserves the multiplicities of the eigenvalues, it follows directly that $\lambda_1^{\sqrt{q}} = \lambda_1^{-1}$ and $\lambda_3^{\sqrt{q}} = \lambda_3^{-1}$. Thus, $\lambda_1^{\sqrt{q}+1} = 1 = \lambda_3^{\sqrt{q}+1}$.
 

{\bf Case 3:}  $P_{U_c}(\lambda)$ has three distinct roots. Let $\{\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \lambda_3\}$ be the set of eigenvalues of $U_c$ over $\overline{\mathbb{F}}_q$. Then the sets $\{\lambda_1^{\sqrt{q}}, \lambda_2^{\sqrt{q}}, \lambda_3^{\sqrt{q}}\}$ and $\{\lambda_1^{-1}, \lambda_2^{-1}, \lambda_3^{-1}\}$ correspond to the eigenvalues of $U_c^*$ and $U_c^{-1}$, respectively. Since these sets must coincide, for each $i \in \{1, 2, 3\}$, we can define a permutation $\tau$ on $\{1, 2, 3\}$ such that $\lambda_i^{\sqrt{q}} = \lambda_{\tau(i)}^{-1}$. Without loss of generality, we may assume that $\tau$ is the identity $(1)$, the transposition $(12)$, or the $3$-cycle $(123)$. 

{\bf Subcase 3.1.} $\tau = (1)$: In this case, $\lambda_i^{\sqrt{q}} = \lambda_i^{-1}$ for all $i=1, 2, 3$, which implies $\lambda_i^{\sqrt{q}+1} = 1$. Each $\lambda_i$ is a $(\sqrt{q}+1)$-th root of unity and thus belongs to $\mathbb{F}_q$. This corresponds to case (iii) in the Theorem.

{\bf Subcase 3.2.} $\tau = (12)$: The relations $\lambda_1^{\sqrt{q}} = \lambda_2^{-1}$, $\lambda_2^{\sqrt{q}} = \lambda_1^{-1}$, and $\lambda_3^{\sqrt{q}} = \lambda_3^{-1}$ imply that $\lambda_3$ is a $(\sqrt{q}+1)$-th root of unity. Furthermore, the first two relations yield:$$\lambda_1^q = (\lambda_1^{\sqrt{q}})^{\sqrt{q}} = (\lambda_2^{-1})^{\sqrt{q}} = (\lambda_2^{\sqrt{q}})^{-1} = (\lambda_1^{-1})^{-1} = \lambda_1.$$Thus, $\lambda_1 \in \mathbb{F}_q$, and similarly, $\lambda_2 \in \mathbb{F}_q$. This aligns with case (iv).

{\bf Subcase 3.3.}  $\tau = (123)$: The relations are given by $\lambda_1^{\sqrt{q}} = \lambda_2^{-1}$, $\lambda_2^{\sqrt{q}} = \lambda_3^{-1}$, and $\lambda_3^{\sqrt{q}} = \lambda_1^{-1}$. We then observe:
$$\lambda_1^q = (\lambda_1^{\sqrt{q}})^{\sqrt{q}} = (\lambda_2^{-1})^{\sqrt{q}} = (\lambda_2^{\sqrt{q}})^{-1} = (\lambda_3^{-1})^{-1} = \lambda_3.$$ By a similar computation, we find $\lambda_2^q = \lambda_1$ and $\lambda_3^q = \lambda_2$. Since the $q$-th power of each $\lambda_i$ is mapped to $\lambda_{\tau(i)}\ne \lambda_i$, no $\lambda_i$ belongs to $\mathbb{F}_q$. Consequently, $P_{U_c}(\lambda)$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{F}_q$ since it is a cubic polynomial.
  
This corresponds to case (v).

body_md:
If $\lambda_0 \in \mathbb{F}_q^*$ is a multiple root of $P_{U_c}(\lambda)$, then 
                                         
$\lambda_0 \in \mu_{\sqrt{q}+1}$ and  the eigenvector corresponding to it represents a point on the curve $C_c$, which is an inflexion.

title: Proof
body_md:
By Case 1 and 2 in the proof of Theorem \ref{5polys}, we have $\lambda_0 \in \mu_{\sqrt{q}+1}$. The eigenvector corresponding $\lambda_0$ is $(\frac{1}{c \lambda_0 }, 1-c^{-\sqrt{q}} \lambda_0 , 1)^t$ by Lemma \ref{eigenvec}. Substituting this vector in the equation of \eqref{eq:Cc}, we have
$$
\begin{aligned}
&\left( \frac{1}{c \lambda_0} \right)^{\sqrt{q}} - c \left( \frac{1}{c \lambda_0} \right) ( (1-c^{-\sqrt{q}}\lambda_0 )^{\sqrt{q}} -1) -   (1 -c^{-\sqrt{q}}\lambda_0 )\\ 
&=\left( \frac{\lambda_0}{c^{\sqrt{q}} } \right)  -   \left( \frac{1}{  \lambda_0} \right)( -c^{-1}\lambda_0 ^{\sqrt{q}}  ) -   (1 -c^{-\sqrt{q}}\lambda_0 )\\ 
&=\left( \frac{1}{c^{\sqrt{q}} \lambda_0^2 } \right) \left( 2 \lambda_0^3 
 - c^{\sqrt{q}} \lambda_0^2 + c^{\sqrt{q}-1}  \right) \\ 
&=\left( \frac{1}{c^{\sqrt{q}} \lambda_0^2 } \right) 
\left(  \lambda_0 P'_{U_c}(\lambda_0) -    P_{U_c}(\lambda_0) \right) =0,
\end{aligned}
$$
where $ P'_{U_c}(\lambda)$ denotes the derivative of $P_{U_c}(\lambda)$.

label: musq
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
To show that the equation has $\sqrt{q}$ distinct roots, we apply Lemma \ref{mathcalY}. Let $y_0 = 1 - c^{-\sqrt{q}}\lambda_0$. First, we verify the norm condition of the coefficient of linear term:
$$\mathrm{Nm}(c((1-c^{-\sqrt{q}}\lambda_0)^{\sqrt{q}}-1))=\mathrm{Nm}(c( -c^{-1}\lambda_0^{\sqrt{q}} ) )= \mathrm{Nm}( -\lambda_0^{\sqrt{q}} )= 1,$$
where we use the relation $\lambda_0^{\sqrt{q}+1}=1$. According to Lemma 17 (iii), it suffices to show that either $y_0 = 0$ or $y_0^{\sqrt{q}-1} + c^{\sqrt{q}}y_0 - c^{\sqrt{q}} = 0$. Note that $y_0 = 0$ if and only if $\lambda_0 = c^{\sqrt{q}}$. In the case where $y_0 \neq 0$ (i.e., $\lambda_0 \neq c^{\sqrt{q}}$), we observe the following:$$\begin{aligned}
y_0^{\sqrt{q}-1} +c^{\sqrt{q}} y_0  - c^{\sqrt{q}}
&= \frac{1}{y_0} \left( y_0^{\sqrt{q}}+c^{\sqrt{q}} y_0^2  - c^{\sqrt{q}}y_0 \right)\\
&=\frac{1}{y_0}\left( (1-c^{-\sqrt{q}} \lambda_0)^{\sqrt{q}}+c^{\sqrt{q}} (1-c^{-\sqrt{q}} \lambda_0)^2  - c^{\sqrt{q}}(1-c^{-\sqrt{q}} \lambda_0) \right)\\
&=\frac{1}{y_0}\left(  1-c^{-1} \lambda_0^{\sqrt{q}}-\lambda_0 +c^{-\sqrt{q}}  \lambda_0^2   \right)\\
&=\frac{1}{y_0} \cdot c^{-\sqrt{q}} \lambda_0^{-1} \left(  c^{\sqrt{q}} \lambda_0 -c^{\sqrt{q}-1} \lambda_0^{\sqrt{q}+1}-c^{\sqrt{q}}\lambda_0^2 +   \lambda_0^3   \right)\\
&=\frac{1}{y_0} \cdot c^{-\sqrt{q}} \lambda_0^{-1} \left(   \lambda_0^3 -c^{\sqrt{q}}\lambda_0^2   +c^{\sqrt{q}} \lambda_0 -c^{\sqrt{q}-1}     \right)\\
&=\frac{1}{y_0} \cdot c^{-\sqrt{q}} \lambda_0^{-1} P_{U_c}(\lambda_0) = 0.
\end{aligned}$$
 
 Therefore, the condition in Lemma \ref{mathcalY} is satisfied, confirming that the equation possesses $\sqrt{q}$ distinct roots.

body_md: By Lemma \ref{musq}, the three corresponding lines are $\sqrt{q}$-lines of $C_c^\circ$, and hence $N_q(C_c) = (q - \sqrt{q} + 1) + 3\sqrt{q}=q +2 \sqrt{q} + 1 $. title: Lemma
body_md: Suppose that $P_{U_c}(\lambda)$ has three distinct roots, exactly one of which belongs to $\mu_{\sqrt{q}+1}$. Then the two eigenvectors corresponding to the other two eigenvalues are inflexions of $C_c$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \lambda_3$ be the three distinct eigenvalues, and assume $\lambda_1 \in \mu_{\sqrt{q}+1}$. According to Theorem \ref{5polys}, this implies $\lambda_2^{\sqrt{q}} = \lambda_3^{-1}$ (and similarly $\lambda_3^{\sqrt{q}} = \lambda_2^{-1}$). From the relation between roots and coefficients of $P_{U_c}(\lambda) = (\lambda-\lambda_1)(\lambda-\lambda_2)(\lambda-\lambda_3)$, we obtain the following system of equations:
\begin{equation}\begin{cases}
\lambda_1 + \lambda_2 + \lambda_3 = c^{\sqrt{q}}, \\ \lambda_1(\lambda_2 + \lambda_3) + \lambda_2\lambda_3 = c^{\sqrt{q}}, \\ \lambda_1\lambda_2\lambda_3 = c^{\sqrt{q}-1}.
\end{cases}\end{equation}
By Lemma \ref{eigenvec}, the eigenvector corresponding to $\lambda_i$ is given by $v_i = ( \frac{1}{c\lambda_i}, 1-c^{-\sqrt{q}}\lambda_i, 1 )^t$. Since the proofs for $i=2$ and $i=3$ are analogous, we only provide the proof for $i=2$. Substituting $v_2$ into the curve equation \eqref{eq:Cc}, we have:
$$\begin{aligned}
&(c \lambda_2 )^{-\sqrt{q}} - \lambda_2^{-1} (1-c^{-1} \lambda_2^{\sqrt{q}}) + \lambda_2^{-1} - (1- c^{-\sqrt{q}}\lambda_2) \\
&= c^{-\sqrt{q}}\lambda_2^{-\sqrt{q}} + c^{-1} \lambda_2^{\sqrt{q}-1} - 1 + c^{-\sqrt{q}}\lambda_2 \\
&= c^{-\sqrt{q}}\lambda_2^{\sqrt{q}-1} \left( \lambda_2^{-2\sqrt{q}+1} + c^{\sqrt{q}-1} - c^{\sqrt{q}}\lambda_2^{-\sqrt{q}+1} + \lambda_2^{-\sqrt{q}+2} \right)\\
&= c^{-\sqrt{q}}\lambda_2^{\sqrt{q}-1} \left( \lambda_2 \lambda_3^2 + c^{\sqrt{q}-1} - c^{\sqrt{q}}\lambda_2 \lambda_3 + \lambda_2^2 \lambda_3 \right)\\
&= c^{-\sqrt{q}}\lambda_2^{\sqrt{q}-1} \left( \lambda_2 \lambda_3 (\lambda_2 + \lambda_3 - c^{\sqrt{q}}) + c^{\sqrt{q}-1} \right)\\
&= c^{-\sqrt{q}}\lambda_2^{\sqrt{q}-1} \left( -\lambda_1 \lambda_2 \lambda_3 + c^{\sqrt{q}-1} \right) = 0.
\end{aligned}$$
The substitution $\lambda_2^{-\sqrt{q}} = \lambda_3$ and the relation $\lambda_1 + \lambda_2 + \lambda_3 = c^{\sqrt{q}}$ were used in the final steps. Thus, $v_2$ is an inflexion point of $C_c$.

label: deg2=1
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{deg2=1}
Let $\alpha, \beta, \gamma \in \mu_{\sqrt{q}+1}$. If $\alpha + \beta + \gamma = c^{\sqrt{q}} = \alpha \beta + \beta \gamma + \alpha \gamma$ for some $c \in \mathbb{F}_q^*$, then it necessarily follows that $\alpha \beta \gamma = c^{\sqrt{q}-1}$. Consequently, such $\alpha, \beta$, and $\gamma$ are precisely the roots of the polynomial $f_c$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\alpha\beta\gamma =d$. We have 
$$ \frac{1}{\alpha} + \frac{1}{\beta} + \frac{1}{\gamma} = \alpha^{\sqrt{q}} +   \beta^{\sqrt{q}} +  \gamma^{\sqrt{q}} = (\alpha+\beta+\gamma)^{\sqrt{q}} =(c^{\sqrt{q}})^{\sqrt{q}} =c.$$ 
On the other hand, we have 
$$ \frac{c^{\sqrt{q}}}{d} = \frac{\alpha\beta +\beta\gamma+\alpha\gamma}{\alpha\beta\gamma} =  \frac{1}{\alpha} + \frac{1}{\beta} + \frac{1}{\gamma} =c.$$
Thus $\alpha\beta\gamma =d= \frac{c^{\sqrt{q}}}{c} =c^{\sqrt{q}-1}$.

label: doublealpha
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{doublealpha} Let $p\ne 3$. For any  $\alpha \in \mu_{\sqrt{q}+1}$, 
there exists a unique element $c \in \mathbb{F}_q^*$ such that $\alpha$ is a double root of the polynomial $f_c$.
Moreover, the remaining root of $f_c(\lambda)$ is given by $\frac{\alpha(2-\alpha)}{2\alpha-1}$, which also belongs to $\mu_{\sqrt{q}+1}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Note that $2^{\sqrt{q}+1}=2^2 \ne 1$ since $p>3$, and hence $2, 2^{-1} \not\in \mu_{\sqrt{q}+1}$. Thus $\frac{\alpha(2-\alpha)}{2\alpha-1}$ is nonzero element in $\mathbb{F}_q$.
First, we observe that
$$\left( \frac{\alpha(2-\alpha)}{2\alpha-1} \right)^{\sqrt{q}} = \frac{\alpha^{\sqrt{q}}(2-\alpha^{\sqrt{q}})}{2\alpha^{\sqrt{q}}-1} = \frac{\alpha^{-1}(2-\alpha^{-1})}{2\alpha^{-1}-1} = \frac{2\alpha-1}{\alpha(2-\alpha)} = \left(\frac{\alpha(2-\alpha)}{2\alpha-1} \right)^{-1},$$
which implies that $\frac{\alpha(2-\alpha)}{2\alpha-1} \in \mu_{\sqrt{q}+1}$. Furthermore, since
$$2\alpha + \frac{\alpha(2-\alpha)}{2\alpha-1} = \frac{3\alpha^2}{2\alpha-1} \quad \text{and} \quad \alpha^2 + 2\alpha \left( \frac{\alpha(2-\alpha)}{2\alpha-1} \right) = \frac{3\alpha^2}{2\alpha-1},$$
the conditions of Lemma \ref{deg2=1} are satisfied. Consequently, the polynomial $f_c$ with $c = \left( \frac{3\alpha^2}{2\alpha-1} \right)^{\sqrt{q}}$ (or $c^{\sqrt{q}} = \frac{3\alpha^2}{2\alpha-1}$) possesses $\alpha$ as a double root and $\frac{\alpha(2-\alpha)}{2\alpha-1}$ as the third root.

Let $f_{c'}$ be a polynomial with $c' \in \mathbb{F}_q$ such that $f_{c'}$ has $\alpha$ as a double root, and let $\beta$ denote the remaining root. Then, the relations between the roots and coefficients imply:
$$2\alpha + \beta = c'^{\sqrt{q}} = \alpha^2 + 2\alpha\beta.
$$
From this equality, we obtain $\beta(2\alpha - 1) = 2\alpha - \alpha^2$, which yields:
$$\beta = \frac{\alpha(2-\alpha)}{2\alpha-1}.$$
This value of $\beta$ is identical to the one derived previously. Consequently, it follows that $c' = c$, establishing the uniqueness of the polynomial $f_c$ that possesses a given $\alpha \in \mu_{\sqrt{q}+1}$ as a double root.

label: p3doubleroot
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{p3doubleroot}
 
When $p=3$, if the polynomial $f_c$ (with $c \neq 0$) possesses a double root $\alpha$, then it must be that 
$\alpha = 2$. Specifically, for $\alpha=2 \in \mu_{\sqrt{q}+1}$ and any $\beta \in \mu_{\sqrt{q}+1} \setminus \{2\}$, the 
polynomial $f_c$ with $c = (1+\beta)^{\sqrt{q}}$ has $2$ as a double root and $\beta$ as the remaining simple root. Note that 
the case $\beta=2$ is excluded because it leads to $c=0$, which contradicts our assumption that $c \in \mathbb{F}_q^*$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If $\alpha$ is a double root of some $f_c$ with $c\neq 0$, then $0=f_c'(\alpha) = -2c^{\sqrt{q}} \alpha + c^{\sqrt{q}}$, which implies that
$\alpha =2$.
 
Note that $2 \in \mu_{\sqrt{q}+1}$.
                                                                                           

Let $f_c$ have $2$ as a double root and $\beta$ as the third root. Then:
$$f_c(\lambda) = (\lambda - 2)^2 (\lambda - \beta) = (\lambda + 1)^2 (\lambda - \beta) = \lambda^3 - (1+\beta)\lambda^2 + (1+\beta)\lambda - \beta.$$
 
Comparing coefficients yields $c^{\sqrt{q}} = 1+\beta$ and $\beta=c^{\sqrt{q}-1}$. Since $c \in \mathbb{F}_q^*$, it follows that $\beta \in \mu_{\sqrt{q}+1}$.
Indeed, one can verify that $2, 2$, and $\beta$ are the roots of $f_c$ with $c = (1+\beta)^{\sqrt{q}}=1+\beta^{\sqrt{q}}$.

has a triple root if and only if 
$\alpha =\frac{\alpha(2-\alpha)}{2\alpha-1}$, which is equivalent to $\alpha =1$ since $\alpha\ne 0$. In fact, when $c=3$, we have
$f_c(\lambda)= \lambda^3 -c^{\sqrt{q}} \lambda^2 + c^{\sqrt{q}} \lambda -c^{\sqrt{q}-1} =  \lambda^3 -3 \lambda^2 + 3 \lambda -1 =(\lambda-1)^3 $.

label: sum1prod1
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{sum1prod1}
Let $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_2$ be distinct elements in $\mathbb{F}_q^*$ satisfying
$\{\alpha_1^{\sqrt{q}}, \alpha_2^{\sqrt{q}}\} = \{\alpha_1^{-1}, \alpha_2^{-1}\}$ and $\alpha_1 + \alpha_2 = 1$.
Then $\alpha_1 \alpha_2 = 1$. In the case where $\alpha_1^{\sqrt{q}}=\alpha_2^{-1}$ and $\alpha_2^{\sqrt{q}}=\alpha_1^{-1}$, we further have $\alpha_1, \alpha_2 \in \mathbb{F}_{\sqrt{q}}^*$.

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $\alpha_1 + \alpha_2 = 1$, we have
\[
1 = (\alpha_1 + \alpha_2)^{\sqrt{q}} = \alpha_1^{\sqrt{q}} + \alpha_2^{\sqrt{q}} = \alpha_1^{-1} + \alpha_2^{-1} = \frac{\alpha_1 + \alpha_2}{\alpha_1 \alpha_2} = \frac{1}{\alpha_1 \alpha_2},
\]
and hence $\alpha_1 \alpha_2 = 1$. 

Finally, if $\alpha_1^{\sqrt{q}} = \alpha_2^{-1}$ and $\alpha_2^{\sqrt{q}} = \alpha_1^{-1}$, we have
\[
\alpha_1^{\sqrt{q}-1} = \alpha_1^{\sqrt{q}} \alpha_1^{-1} = \alpha_2^{-1} \alpha_1^{-1} = (\alpha_1 \alpha_2)^{-1} = 1.
\]
Similarly, it follows that $\alpha_2^{\sqrt{q}-1} = 1$, which implies $\alpha_1, \alpha_2 \in \mathbb{F}_{\sqrt{q}}^*$.

label: thirdone
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{thirdone}
Let $\alpha, \beta \in \mu_{\sqrt{q}+1}$. Suppose that $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are roots of $f_c(\lambda)$ for some $c \in \mathbb{F}_q^*$.
\begin{enumerate}[\rm(i)]
\item If $\alpha + \beta \neq 1$ and $\alpha^2 + \alpha\beta + \beta^2 \neq 0$, then the third root $\gamma$ also belongs to $\mu_{\sqrt{q}+1}$. In this case, $\gamma$ and $c$ are explicitly given by
$$\gamma = \frac{\alpha + \beta - \alpha\beta}{\alpha + \beta - 1} \quad \text{and} \quad c = \left( \frac{\alpha^2 + \alpha\beta + \beta^2}{\alpha + \beta - 1} \right)^{\sqrt{q}}.$$
\item If $\alpha + \beta = 1$, then,                                                               
for any $\gamma \in \mu_{\sqrt{q}+1} \setminus \{-1\}$, the elements $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ are the roots of $f_c(\lambda)$ with $c = (1 + \gamma)^{\sqrt{q}} = 1 + \gamma^{\sqrt{q}}$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
(i) Let $\gamma = \frac{\alpha + \beta - \alpha\beta}{\alpha + \beta - 1}$. Then we have:
$$\gamma^{\sqrt{q}} = \left( \frac{\alpha + \beta - \alpha\beta}{\alpha + \beta - 1} \right)^{\sqrt{q}} = \frac{\alpha^{-1} + \beta^{-1} - \alpha^{-1}\beta^{-1}}{\alpha^{-1} + \beta^{-1} - 1} = \frac{\alpha + \beta - 1}{\alpha + \beta - \alpha\beta} = \gamma^{-1},$$
which implies $\gamma^{\sqrt{q}+1} = 1$. Furthermore, a direct calculation shows that:
$$\alpha + \beta + \gamma = \alpha + \beta + \frac{\alpha + \beta - \alpha\beta}{\alpha + \beta - 1} = 
                                                                                                  
 \frac{\alpha^2 + \alpha\beta + \beta^2}{\alpha + \beta - 1},$$
and
$$                
\alpha\beta + \beta\gamma + \alpha\gamma   
= \alpha\beta + (\alpha + \beta)\gamma = \alpha\beta + (\alpha + \beta) \frac{\alpha + \beta - \alpha\beta}{\alpha + \beta - 1}    
                                                                                                                  
= \frac{\alpha^2 + \alpha\beta + \beta^2}{\alpha + \beta - 1}.
              
$$
By Lemma \ref{deg2=1}, it follows that $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ are the roots of the polynomial $\lambda^3 - c^{\sqrt{q}}\lambda^2 + c^{\sqrt{q}}\lambda - c^{\sqrt{q}-1}$ where $c = \left( \frac{\alpha^2 + \alpha\beta + \beta^2}{\alpha + \beta - 1} \right)^{\sqrt{q}}$.

(ii) If we let $\alpha + \beta = 1$, then $\alpha\beta=1$ by Lemma \ref{sum1prod1}. 
 
Let $\gamma \in \mu_{\sqrt{q}+1} \setminus \{-1\}$ and set $c = (1 + \gamma)^{\sqrt{q}} = 1 + \gamma^{\sqrt{q}}$. Then we have:
$$\alpha + \beta + \gamma = 1 + \gamma = (1 + \gamma)^{q} = c^{\sqrt{q}},$$
and
$$\alpha\beta + \beta\gamma + \alpha\gamma = 1 + \gamma(\alpha + \beta) = 1 + \gamma = c^{\sqrt{q}}.$$
By Lemma \ref{deg2=1}, $\alpha, \beta$, and $\gamma$ are indeed the roots of the polynomial $f_c$ for $c = (1 + \gamma)^{\sqrt{q}}$.
head: environment

label: sum1a2abb20
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{sum1a2abb20} If $\alpha + \beta = 1$, then $\alpha\beta = 1$ and                                        
$\alpha^2 + \alpha\beta + \beta^2=(\alpha + \beta)^2 - \alpha\beta = 1^2 - 1 = 0$.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: In the context of Lemma \ref{thirdone} (2), the condition $\gamma \neq -1$ is assumed because $c = 0$ if $\gamma = -1$. Suppose $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are $(\sqrt{q}+1)$-th roots of unity satisfying $\alpha + \beta = 1$ and $\alpha\beta = 1$. In this case, $\alpha^2 + \alpha\beta + \beta^2 = (\alpha + \beta)^2 - \alpha\beta = 1 - 1 = 0$. For any $q$ odd, there exist exactly $\sqrt{q}$ distinct $(\sqrt{q}+1)$-th roots of unity $\gamma$ (excluding $-1$) such that $\alpha, \beta$, and $\gamma$ serve as the roots of the polynomial$$f_c(\lambda) = \lambda^3 - c^{\sqrt{q}}\lambda^2 + c^{\sqrt{q}}\lambda - c^{\sqrt{q}-1}.$$Note that $\gamma$ may coincide with $\alpha$ or $\beta$, which corresponds to the case where the polynomial $f_c(\lambda)$ possesses a multiple root.
head: environment

label: betgamconj
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{betgamconj}
Let $\alpha\in\mu_{\sqrt{q}+1}$. Let $\beta$ and $\gamma$ be elements in $\mathbb{F}_q$ satisfying $\gamma = \beta^{-\sqrt{q}}$. If
$$\alpha + \beta + \gamma = c^{\sqrt{q}} = \alpha\beta + \beta\gamma + \gamma\alpha$$
for some $c \in \mathbb{F}_q$, then $\alpha\beta\gamma = c^{\sqrt{q}-1}$. In particular, $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ are the roots of the polynomial
$$f_c(\lambda) = \lambda^3 - c^{\sqrt{q}}\lambda^2 + c^{\sqrt{q}}\lambda - c^{\sqrt{q}-1}.$$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\alpha\beta\gamma = d$. Since $\alpha \in \mu_{\sqrt{q}+1}$, we have $\alpha^{-1} = \alpha^{\sqrt{q}}$. From the condition $\gamma = \beta^{-\sqrt{q}}$, it follows that $\gamma^{-1} = \beta^{\sqrt{q}}$ and $\beta^{-1} = \gamma^{\sqrt{q}}$. 
The remainder of the proof proceeds by an argument similar to that of Lemma \ref{deg2=1}.
head: environment

label: betgamconjfc
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{betgamconjfc}              
Let $\beta$ and $\gamma$ be elements in $\mathbb{F}_q$ such that $\beta^{\sqrt{q}} = \gamma^{-1}$ (or equivalently, $\beta \gamma^{\sqrt{q}} = 1$).
\begin{enumerate}[\rm (i)]
\item If $\beta + \gamma \neq 1$ and $\beta^2 + \beta\gamma + \gamma^2 \neq 0$, let
$$\alpha = \frac{\beta + \gamma - \beta\gamma}{\beta + \gamma - 1}.$$
Then $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ are the roots of the polynomial
$$\lambda^3 - c^{\sqrt{q}}\lambda^2 + c^{\sqrt{q}}\lambda - c^{\sqrt{q}-1} \quad \text{for} \quad c = \left( \frac{\beta^2 + \beta\gamma + \gamma^2}{\beta + \gamma - 1} \right)^{\sqrt{q}}.$$
Moreover, $\alpha$ is a $(\sqrt{q}+1)$-th root of unity.
\item If $\beta + \gamma = 1$, then                                                      
the roots of the polynomial
$$\lambda^3 - c^{\sqrt{q}}\lambda^2 + c^{\sqrt{q}}\lambda - c^{\sqrt{q}-1}$$
are $\{c^{\sqrt{q}-1}, \beta, \gamma\}$, where $c$ satisfies the equation $c^{\sqrt{q}} - c^{\sqrt{q}-1} - 1 = 0$. Indeed, this equation has exactly $\sqrt{q}$ distinct roots for such $c$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
(i)  Assume $\beta + \gamma \neq 1$ and $\beta^2 + \beta\gamma + \gamma^2 \neq 0$. Let $\alpha$ be defined as:
$$\alpha = \frac{\beta + \gamma - \beta\gamma}{\beta + \gamma - 1}.$$
First, we verify that $\alpha$ is a $(\sqrt{q}+1)$-th root of unity. Taking the $\sqrt{q}$-th power of $\alpha$ and substituting the relations $\beta^{\sqrt{q}} = \gamma^{-1}$ and $\gamma^{\sqrt{q}} = \beta^{-1}$, we obtain:
$$\alpha^{\sqrt{q}} = \frac{\beta^{\sqrt{q}} + \gamma^{\sqrt{q}} - \beta^{\sqrt{q}}\gamma^{\sqrt{q}}}{\beta^{\sqrt{q}} + \gamma^{\sqrt{q}} - 1} = \frac{\gamma^{-1} + \beta^{-1} - \gamma^{-1}\beta^{-1}}{\gamma^{-1} + \beta^{-1} - 1} = \frac{\beta + \gamma - 1}{\beta + \gamma - \beta\gamma} = \alpha^{-1}.$$
Thus, $\alpha^{\sqrt{q}+1} = 1$, confirming $\alpha \in \mu_{\sqrt{q}+1}$. Next, we evaluate the elementary symmetric polynomials. For $c = \left( \frac{\beta^2 + \beta\gamma + \gamma^2}{\beta + \gamma - 1} \right)^{\sqrt{q}}$, we have:
$$\alpha + \beta + \gamma = \frac{\beta + \gamma - \beta\gamma}{\beta + \gamma - 1} + \beta + \gamma = \frac{\beta^2 + \beta\gamma + \gamma^2}{\beta + \gamma - 1} = c^{\sqrt{q}},$$
and
$$\alpha\beta + \beta\gamma + \gamma\alpha = \alpha(\beta + \gamma) + \beta\gamma = \frac{\beta + \gamma - \beta\gamma}{\beta + \gamma - 1}(\beta + \gamma) + \beta\gamma = \frac{\beta^2 + \beta\gamma + \gamma^2}{\beta + \gamma - 1} = c^{\sqrt{q}}.$$
Finally, let $d = \alpha\beta\gamma$. We observe that:$$\frac{c^{\sqrt{q}}}{d} = \frac{\alpha\beta + \beta\gamma + \gamma\alpha}{\alpha\beta\gamma} = \frac{1}{\gamma} + \frac{1}{\alpha} + \frac{1}{\beta} = \alpha^{\sqrt{q}} + \gamma^{\sqrt{q}} + \beta^{\sqrt{q}} = (\alpha + \gamma + \beta)^{\sqrt{q}} = (c^{\sqrt{q}})^{\sqrt{q}} = c.$$It follows that $\alpha\beta\gamma = d = c^{\sqrt{q}-1}$. By the relations of roots and coefficients, $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ are indeed the roots of $\lambda^3 - c^{\sqrt{q}}\lambda^2 + c^{\sqrt{q}}\lambda - c^{\sqrt{q}-1}$.

(ii) If $\beta + \gamma = 1$, then $\beta\gamma =1$ and $\beta,\gamma \in \mathbb{F}_{\sqrt{q}}^*$ by Lemma \ref{sum1prod1}.
 
Let $c$ be an element in $\mathbb{F}_q$ satisfying the equation $c^{\sqrt{q}} - c^{\sqrt{q}-1} - 1 = 0$. 
Since $c^{\sqrt{q}-1} + (\beta + \gamma) = c^{\sqrt{q}-1} + 1 = c^{\sqrt{q}}$ and
$c^{\sqrt{q}-1}(\beta + \gamma) + \beta\gamma = c^{\sqrt{q}-1} + 1 = c^{\sqrt{q}}$,
 
three elements $c^{\sqrt{q}-1}, \beta, \gamma$ are the roots of the polynomial $\lambda^3 - c^{\sqrt{q}}\lambda^2 + c^{\sqrt{q}}\lambda - c^{\sqrt{q}-1}$. Finally, we note that the equation $c^{\sqrt{q}} - c^{\sqrt{q}-1} - 1 = 0$ can be rewritten as $-c^{\sqrt{q}}(-1 + \frac{1}{c} + \frac{1}{c^{\sqrt{q}}}) = 0$. Since $(-1)^{1-\sqrt{q}} = 1$ for any $q$, according to Proposition \ref{degsqrtq}, this equation possesses exactly $\sqrt{q}$ distinct roots.
head: environment

label: 3rdroot
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{3rdroot}
Let $\mu_3$ be the group of the third roots of unity,
which is a subgroup of $\mathbb{F}_q^{\ast}$.
\begin{enumerate}[\rm(i)]
\item If $\sqrt{q} \equiv 0 \pmod 3$, then $\mu_3 = \{1\}$.
\item If $\sqrt{q} \not\equiv 0 \pmod 3$, then
$|\mu_3| =3$, and
\begin{enumerate}[\rm(a)]
\item $\mu_3 \subset \mu_{\sqrt{q}+1}$ if and only if
$\sqrt{q} \equiv 2 \pmod 3$;
\item $\mu_3 \subset \mathbb{F}_{\sqrt{q}}^{\ast}$
if and only if
$\sqrt{q} \equiv 1 \pmod 3$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The assertions (i) and the first part of (ii) are trivial.
The remaining parts come from
the representations of groups:
$\mathbb{F}_q^{\ast}= \langle \omega \rangle$,
$\mu_{\sqrt{q}+1} =\langle \omega^{\sqrt{q}-1}\rangle$,
$\mathbb{F}_{\sqrt{q}}^{\ast} = \langle \omega^{\sqrt{q}+1}\rangle$
and $\mu_3 =\langle \omega^{\frac{q-1}{3}}\rangle$.
head: environment

label: mua+b=1
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{mua+b=1}
Let $\alpha, \beta \in \mu_{\sqrt{q}+1}$ and $\alpha + \beta = 1$. 
 
Then                       
the following hold:
\begin{enumerate}[\rm(i)]
\item The case $q \equiv 0 \pmod 2$ (Characteristic $p=2$): If $\sqrt{q} \equiv 2 \pmod 3$, then the solutions are:
$$\begin{cases} \alpha = \omega^{\frac{q-1}{3}} \\ \beta = \alpha^{-1} = \omega^{\frac{2(q-1)}{3}} \end{cases} \quad \text{or} \quad \begin{cases} \alpha = \omega^{\frac{2(q-1)}{3}} \\ \beta = \alpha^{-1} = \omega^{\frac{q-1}{3}} \end{cases}$$
If $\sqrt{q} \equiv 1 \pmod 3$, then there is no solution.
\item The case $q \equiv 0 \pmod 3$ (Characteristic $p=3$): The only solution is $\alpha = \beta = 2$.
\item The other cases ($p \neq 2, 3$): If $\sqrt{q} \equiv 2 \pmod 3$, then the solutions are:
$$\begin{cases} \alpha = \omega^{\frac{q-1}{6}} \\ \beta = \alpha^{-1} = \omega^{\frac{5(q-1)}{6}} \end{cases} \quad \text{or} \quad \begin{cases} \alpha = \omega^{\frac{5(q-1)}{6}} \\ \beta = \alpha^{-1} = \omega^{\frac{q-1}{6}} \end{cases}$$
If $\sqrt{q} \equiv 1 \pmod 3$, then there is no solution.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $\alpha+\beta=1$, we have $\alpha\beta=1$ by Lemma \ref{sum1prod1}. 

\noindent (i) By Lemma \ref{prodsum1}, $\{\alpha,\beta\}=
\{\omega^{\frac{q-1}{3}},\omega^{\frac{2(q-1)}{3}}\}\subseteq \mu_3$. By Lemma \ref{3rdroot}, (i) follows.
 
  

\noindent (ii) follows from Lemma \ref{prodsum1}.
 
 
\noindent (iii) By Lemma \ref{prodsum1}, $\{\alpha,\beta\}=
\{\omega^{\frac{q-1}{6}},\omega^{-\frac{q-1}{6}}\}$. 
Notice that $\omega^{\pm \frac{q-1}{6}} \in \mu_{\sqrt{q}+1}$ if and only if 
$\left(\omega^{\pm \frac{q-1}{6}}\right)^{\sqrt{q}+1} = 1$, 
which is equivalent to $\sqrt{q}+1 \equiv 0 \pmod{6}$. 
Since $q$ is odd, this is further equivalent to $\sqrt{q}+1 \equiv 0 \pmod{3}$. Now (iii) follows from Lemma \ref{3rdroot}.
head: environment

label: conja+b=1
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{conja+b=1}
Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be elements in $\mathbb{F}_q$ such that $\alpha^{\sqrt{q}} = \beta^{-1}$ and $\alpha + \beta = 1$. Then the following hold:
\begin{enumerate}[\rm (i)]
\item Case $q \equiv 0 \pmod 2$: If $\sqrt{q} \equiv 1 \pmod 3$, the solutions are:
$$\begin{cases} \alpha = \omega^{\frac{q-1}{3}} \\ \beta = \alpha^{-1} = \omega^{\frac{2(q-1)}{3}} \end{cases} \quad \text{or} \quad \begin{cases} \alpha = \omega^{\frac{2(q-1)}{3}} \\ \beta = \alpha^{-1} = \omega^{\frac{q-1}{3}} \end{cases}$$
If $\sqrt{q} \equiv 2 \pmod 3$, there is no solution.

\item Case $q \equiv 0 \pmod 3$: The unique solution is $\alpha = \beta = 2$, which belongs to the group of $(\sqrt{q}+1)$-th roots of unity, $\mu_{\sqrt{q}+1}$.

\item Case $p \neq 2, 3$: If $\sqrt{q} \equiv 1 \pmod 3$, the solutions are:
$$\begin{cases} \alpha = \omega^{\frac{q-1}{6}} \\ \beta = \alpha^{-1} = \omega^{\frac{5(q-1)}{6}} \end{cases} \quad \text{or} \quad \begin{cases} \alpha = \omega^{\frac{5(q-1)}{6}} \\ \beta = \alpha^{-1} = \omega^{\frac{q-1}{6}} \end{cases}$$
If $\sqrt{q} \equiv 2 \pmod 3$, there is no solution.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: By Lemma \ref{sum1prod1}, $\alpha\beta=1$ and $\alpha,\beta \in\mathbb{F}_{\sqrt{q}}^*$. Now, using Lemma \ref{prodsum1} and Lemma \ref{3rdroot}, we can proceed with the proof in a similar manner to that of Lemma \ref{mua+b=1}.
head: environment

label: ma2+ab+b2=0
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{ma2+ab+b2=0}
Consider the equation $\alpha^2 + \alpha\beta + \beta^2 = 0$ for $\alpha, \beta \in \mu_{\sqrt{q}+1}$.
\begin{enumerate}[\rm(i)]
\item If $\sqrt{q} \equiv 0 \pmod 3$, the equation is satisfied if and only if $\alpha = \beta$.
\item If $\sqrt{q} \equiv 1 \pmod 3$, there is no such $\alpha, \beta \in \mu_{\sqrt{q}+1}$ satisfying the equation.  
                                                     
\item If $\sqrt{q} \equiv 2 \pmod 3$, the solutions are given by $\beta = \alpha \omega^{\frac{q-1}{3}}$ and $\beta = \alpha \omega^{\frac{2(q-1)}{3}}$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $\alpha^3 - \beta^3 = (\alpha - \beta)(\alpha^2 + \alpha\beta + \beta^2) = 0$, we have $\beta = \alpha\zeta$ for some $\zeta \in \mu_3$.
If $p = 3$, i.e., $\sqrt{q} \equiv 0\pmod{3}$, then $\zeta = 1$, which implies $\alpha = \beta$.
When $p \neq 3$, $\zeta\in\mu_3 \setminus \{1\}$, and  we obtain (ii) and (iii), by Lemma \ref{3rdroot}.
head: environment

label: conja2+ab+b2=0
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{conja2+ab+b2=0}
Consider the equation $\alpha^2 + \alpha\beta + \beta^2 = 0$ for $\alpha, \beta \in \mathbb{F}_q$ such that $\alpha^{\sqrt{q}} = \beta^{-1}$. Then the following hold:
\begin{enumerate}[\rm(i)]
\item If $\sqrt{q} \equiv 0 \pmod 3$, the equation is satisfied if and only if $\alpha = \beta$. In this case, $\alpha$ (and thus $\beta$) necessarily belongs to $\mu_{\sqrt{q}+1}$.
\item If $\sqrt{q} \equiv 2 \pmod 3$, there are no such $\alpha$ and $\beta$ satisfying the given conditions.
\item If $\sqrt{q} \equiv 1 \pmod 3$, the solutions are given by $\beta = \alpha \omega^{\frac{q-1}{3}}$ or $\beta = \alpha \omega^{\frac{2(q-1)}{3}}$. In this case, the number of such $(\alpha,\beta)$'s is $2(\sqrt{q}+1)$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
As in the proof of Lemma~\ref{ma2+ab+b2=0}, we have $\beta = \alpha\zeta$ for some $\zeta \in \mu_3$.
When $p = 3$, we have $\zeta = 1$ and $\alpha = \beta$, which implies $\alpha \in \mu_{\sqrt{q}+1}$.
When $p \neq 3$, we have $\zeta \in \mu_3 \setminus \{1\}$. Substituting $\beta = \alpha\zeta$ into $\alpha^{\sqrt{q}} = \beta^{-1}$ yields $\zeta = \alpha^{ \sqrt{q}+1 } \in \mathbb{F}_{\sqrt{q}}$. Thus, $\zeta \in \mathbb{F}_{\sqrt{q}}^*$.

Now, applying Lemma~\ref{3rdroot}, we obtain (ii) and the first assertion of (iii). 
For each $\zeta \in \mu_3 \setminus \{1\} = \{\omega^{\pm \frac{q-1}{3}}\}$, the equation $\alpha^{\sqrt{q}+1} = \zeta$ in $\alpha$ has $\sqrt{q}+1$ solutions in $\mathbb{F}_q$. 
Hence, the second assertion of (iii) follows.
head: environment

label: S1S2S3
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $(\alpha, \beta, \gamma) \in S_1$. From the relations $\alpha + \beta + \gamma = c^{\sqrt{q}}$ and $\alpha\beta + \beta\gamma + \alpha\gamma = c^{\sqrt{q}}$, we obtain the identity:
$$\gamma(\alpha + \beta - 1) = \alpha + \beta - \alpha\beta$$

Case 1: $\alpha + \beta \neq 1$. In this case, $\gamma = \frac{\alpha + \beta - \alpha\beta}{\alpha + \beta - 1}$. Since $c \neq 0$, the relation $c^{\sqrt{q}} = \frac{\alpha^2 + \alpha\beta + \beta^2}{\alpha + \beta - 1}$ implies $\alpha^2 + \alpha\beta + \beta^2 \neq 0$. Thus, $(\alpha, \beta, \gamma) \in S_2$.

Case 2: $\alpha + \beta = 1$ . The relation $c^{\sqrt{q}} = \alpha + \beta + \gamma = 1 + \gamma$ implies $\gamma \neq -1$ since $c \neq 0$. Thus, $(\alpha, \beta, \gamma) \in S_3$.

Therefore, $S_1 \subseteq S_2 \cup S_3$.

Now we prove $S_2 \cup S_3 \subseteq S_1$. If $(\alpha, \beta, \gamma) \in S_2$, let $c = \left( \frac{\alpha^2 + \alpha\beta + \beta^2}{\alpha + \beta - 1} \right)^{\sqrt{q}}$. Then $\alpha + \beta + \gamma = c^{\sqrt{q}} = \alpha\beta + \beta\gamma + \alpha\gamma$. Since $\frac{c^{\sqrt{q}}}{\alpha\beta\gamma} = \frac{1}{\alpha} + \frac{1}{\beta} + \frac{1}{\gamma} = (\alpha + \beta + \gamma)^{\sqrt{q}} = c$, we obtain $\alpha\beta\gamma = c^{\sqrt{q}-1}$. Thus, $S_2 \subseteq S_1$. If $(\alpha, \beta, \gamma) \in S_3$, then, since $\alpha + \beta = 1$ and $\alpha, \beta \in \mu_{\sqrt{q}+1}$, we have $1 = (\alpha + \beta)^{\sqrt{q}} = \frac{1}{\alpha} + \frac{1}{\beta} = \frac{1}{\alpha\beta}$, which implies $\alpha\beta = 1$. Setting $c = (1 + \gamma)^{\sqrt{q}}$ leads to $c^{\sqrt{q}} = 1 + \gamma = \alpha\beta + \beta\gamma + \alpha\gamma$ and $\alpha\beta\gamma = c^{\sqrt{q}-1}$ by the same logic as above. Thus, $S_3 \subseteq S_1$. Consequently, $S_2 \cup S_3 \subseteq S_1$.

Thus the equality $S_1 = S_2 \cup S_3$ is proved.
head: environment

label: polysq03
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{polysq03}
Assume that $\sqrt{q} \equiv 0 \pmod{3}$. Under this condition, we observe the following properties regarding the  polynomials $f_c$:

\begin{enumerate}[\rm(i)]
    \item There exists no polynomial $f_c$ with $c \neq 0$ that possesses a triple root.
    
    \item The number of polynomials $f_c$ having a double root is $\sqrt{q}$. In this case, both the double root and the remaining simple root belong to
    $\mu_{\sqrt{q}+1}$.
    
    \item The number of polynomials $f_c$ that have three distinct roots, all of which belong to
    $\mu_{\sqrt{q}+1}$,
    is given by $\dfrac{q-\sqrt{q}}{6}$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
(i) By Theorem \ref{5polys}, there exists no $f_c$ with $c\ne 0$ that possesses a triple root. 
(ii) By Lemma \ref{p3doubleroot}, for each $\beta \in \mu_{\sqrt{q}+1} \setminus \{2\}$, if $c = (1+\beta)^{\sqrt{q}}$, then the polynomial $f_c$ possesses a double root at $2$ and a simple root at $\beta$. Furthermore, these are the only polynomials $f_c$ (with $c \neq 0$) that possess a double root in characteristic $3$.
Therefore, there are exactly $\sqrt{q}$ polynomials $f_c$ (with $c \in \mathbb{F}_q^*$) that possess a double root but not a triple root. 

(iii) For each $\beta \in \mu_{\sqrt{q}+1} \setminus \{2\}$, the triples $(2, 2, \beta)$, $(2, \beta, 2)$, and $(\beta, 2, 2)$ are elements of $S_1$, defined in Lemma \ref{S1S2S3}, and correspond to the roots of the same polynomial $f_c$. Consequently, the total number of triples in $S_1$ arising from these $\sqrt{q}$ polynomials with double roots is $3\sqrt{q}$.
Since $S_1 = S_2 \cup S_3$ is a disjoint union, we determine $|S_1|$ by calculating $|S_2|$ and $|S_3|$ independently.

1. Cardinality of $S_2$: The elements of $S_2$ are determined by pairs $(\alpha, \beta) \in \mu_{\sqrt{q}+1}^2$ satisfying $\alpha + \beta - 1 \neq 0$ and $\alpha^2 + \alpha\beta + \beta^2 \neq 0$. By Lemma \ref{mua+b=1}, if $\alpha + \beta = 1$, then $\alpha\beta = 1$, which implies $\alpha^2 + \alpha\beta + \beta^2 = (\alpha+\beta)^2 - \alpha\beta = 1 - 1 = 0$. Thus, it suffices to count pairs satisfying $\alpha^2 + \alpha\beta + \beta^2 \neq 0$. According to Lemma \ref{ma2+ab+b2=0}, the condition $\alpha^2 + \alpha\beta + \beta^2 = 0$ holds if and only if $\alpha = \beta$ (in characteristic 3). Since there are $\sqrt{q}+1$ such pairs, we have:
$$|S_2| = (\sqrt{q}+1)^2 - (\sqrt{q}+1) = q + \sqrt{q}$$

2. Cardinality of $S_3$: For $S_3$, Lemma \ref{mua+b=1} states that $\alpha + \beta = 1$ implies $\alpha = \beta = 2$. For this fixed pair, there are exactly $\sqrt{q}$ choices for $\gamma \in \mu_{\sqrt{q}+1} \setminus \{-1\}$. Thus: 
$$|S_3| = \sqrt{q}.$$

3. Total Cardinality and Number of Polynomials: Therefore, the total number of triples in $S_1$ is:
$$|S_1| = (q + \sqrt{q}) + \sqrt{q} = q + 2\sqrt{q}.$$
As previously noted, $S_1$ contains no triples with three identical components. The number of triples with exactly two identical components is $3\sqrt{q}$. Subtracting these, the number of triples consisting of three distinct elements is:$$(q + 2\sqrt{q}) - 3\sqrt{q} = q - \sqrt{q}$$Since each such triple has $3! = 6$ permutations that correspond to the same set of roots for a single polynomial $f_c$, the number of distinct polynomials $f_c$ possessing three distinct roots in $\mu_{\sqrt{q}+1}$ is:
$$\frac{q - \sqrt{q}}{6}.$$

label: polysq13
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{polysq13}
Assume that $\sqrt{q} \equiv 1 \pmod{3}$. Under this condition, we observe the following properties regarding the characteristic polynomials $f_c$:

\begin{enumerate}[\rm(i)]
    \item There exists a unique polynomial $f_c$ with $c \neq 0$ that has a triple root. In this case, the triple root is 1 and $c=3$ (or $c=1$ if $p=2$).
    
    \item The number of polynomials $f_c$ having a double root is $\sqrt{q}$. In this case, both the double root and the remaining simple root belong to
    $\mu_{\sqrt{q}+1}$.
    
    \item The number of polynomials $f_c$ that have three distinct roots, all of which belong to
    $\mu_{\sqrt{q}+1}$,
    is given by $\dfrac{q-\sqrt{q}}{6}$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The proof follows the same lines as that of Lemma \ref{polysq03} with slight modifications. (i) By Theorem \ref{5polys}, there exists a unique $f_c$ with $c \neq 0$ that possesses a triple root. Specifically, for $c=3$, the triple root is $\alpha=1$, and $(1,1,1) \in S_1$. 

(ii) By Lemma \ref{doublealpha} and Lemma \ref{p3doubleroot}, there are exactly $\sqrt{q}$ polynomials $f_c$ (with $c \neq 0$), each of which possesses a double root $\alpha \in \mu_{\sqrt{q}+1} \setminus \{1\}$ and a third root $\frac{\alpha(2-\alpha)}{2\alpha - 1} \in \mu_{\sqrt{q}+1}$. 

(iii) The total number of triples in $S_1$ arising from these $\sqrt{q}$ polynomials with double roots is $3\sqrt{q}$.
Since $S_1 = S_2 \cup S_3$ is a disjoint union, we determine $|S_1|$ by calculating $|S_2|$ and $|S_3|$ independently.

1. Cardinality of $S_2$: The elements of $S_2$ are determined by pairs $(\alpha, \beta) \in \mu_{\sqrt{q}+1}^2$ satisfying $\alpha + \beta - 1 \neq 0$ and $\alpha^2 + \alpha\beta + \beta^2 \neq 0$. By Lemma \ref{mua+b=1}, if $\alpha + \beta = 1$, then $\alpha\beta = 1$, which implies $\alpha^2 + \alpha\beta + \beta^2 = 0$. Thus, it suffices to count pairs satisfying $\alpha^2 + \alpha\beta + \beta^2 \neq 0$. According to Lemma \ref{ma2+ab+b2=0}, the condition $\alpha^2 + \alpha\beta + \beta^2 = 0$ has no solutions. Thus  we have:
$$|S_2| = (\sqrt{q}+1)^2 $$

2. Cardinality of $S_3$: For $S_3$, Lemma \ref{mua+b=1} states that $\alpha + \beta = 1$ has no solution, and hence 
$$|S_3| =0$$

3. Total Cardinality and Number of Polynomials: Therefore, the total number of triples in $S_1$ is:
$$|S_1| = ( \sqrt{q}+1)^2$$
As previously noted, $S_1$ contains only one triple $(1,1,1)$ with three identical components. The number of triples with exactly two identical components is $3\sqrt{q}$. Subtracting these, the number of triples consisting of three distinct elements is:
$$( 2\sqrt{q}+1)^2 -1 - 3\sqrt{q} = q - \sqrt{q}.$$
Thus the number of distinct polynomials $f_c$ possessing three distinct roots in $\mu_{\sqrt{q}+1}$ is:
$$\frac{q - \sqrt{q}}{6}.$$

\end{enumerate}

body_md:
By Theorem \ref{5polys}, if the characteristic polynomial of $A$ has three distinct roots $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ such that only $\alpha$ is a $(\sqrt{q}+1)$-th root of unity, then $\beta$ and $\gamma$ satisfy $\beta \neq \gamma$ and $\beta^{\sqrt{q}} = \gamma^{-1}$. The number of such pairs $\{\beta, \gamma\} = \{\beta, \beta^{-\sqrt{q}}\}$ is exactly
$$\frac{q - 1 - (\sqrt{q} + 1)}{2} = \frac{q - \sqrt{q} - 2}{2}.$$
Following the argument in Lemma \ref{betgamconjfc}, for each pair $\{\beta, \gamma\}$, the value of $\alpha$ is determined based on the following conditions:If $\beta + \gamma \neq 1$ and $\beta^2 + \beta\gamma + \gamma^2 \neq 0$: The value of $\alpha$ is uniquely determined as
$$\alpha = \frac{\beta + \gamma - \beta\gamma}{\beta + \gamma - 1}.$$
If $\beta + \gamma = 1$, by Lemma \ref{betgamconjfc}, there are exactly $\sqrt{q}$ possible values for $\alpha$.

In the case where $\sqrt{q} \equiv 0 \pmod 3$, Lemma \ref{conja+b=1} and Lemma \ref{ma2+ab+b2=0} imply that $\beta + \gamma = 1$ holds if and only if $\beta = \gamma = 2$, and $\beta^2 + \beta\gamma + \gamma^2 = 0$ holds only when $\beta = \gamma$. Since we are considering the case where $\beta \neq \gamma$, 
for each pair  $(\beta, \gamma)$ of the $\frac{q - \sqrt{q} - 2}{2}$ pairs, $\alpha$ is uniquely determined. Thus, the total number of such characteristic polynomials is $\frac{q - \sqrt{q} - 2}{2}$.
 

In the case where $\sqrt{q} \equiv 1 \pmod{3}$, the enumeration of the characteristic polynomials is conducted as follows. First, the number of pairs $(\beta, \gamma)$ such that $\beta^{\sqrt{q}} = \gamma^{-1}$ and $\beta \neq \gamma$ is $q - \sqrt{q} - 2$.  By Remark \ref{sum1a2abb20},   the condition $\beta + \gamma = 1$ implies $\beta^2 + \beta\gamma + \gamma^2 = 0$. By Lemma \ref{conja2+ab+b2=0}, the number of pairs $(\beta, \gamma)$ satisfying both $\beta^2 + \beta\gamma + \gamma^2 \neq 0$ and $\beta + \gamma \neq 1$ is calculated by:
$$(q - \sqrt{q} - 2) - 2(\sqrt{q} + 1) = q - 3\sqrt{q} - 4.$$ 
For each such pair $(\beta, \gamma)$, the root $\alpha$ is uniquely determined.
On the other hand, by Lemma \ref{conja+b=1}, there are exactly two pairs that satisfy the condition $\beta + \gamma = 1$. For each of these pairs, Lemma \ref{betgamconjfc} implies that there are $\sqrt{q}$ possible values for $\alpha$.
Consequently, the total number of triples $(\alpha, \beta, \gamma)$ such that $f_c(\alpha) = f_c(\beta) = f_c(\gamma) = 0$ for some $c \in \mathbb{F}_q^*$ is:
$$(q - 3\sqrt{q} - 4) + 2\sqrt{q} = q - \sqrt{q} - 4.$$
Since the characteristic polynomials corresponding to the triples $(\alpha, \beta, \gamma)$ and $(\alpha, \gamma, \beta)$ are identical, the total number of distinct characteristic polynomials is
$\frac{q - \sqrt{q} - 4}{2}.$

When $\sqrt{q} \equiv 2 \pmod 3$:
By Lemma \ref{conja+b=1} and Lemma \ref{ma2+ab+b2=0}, there exist no $\beta, \gamma$ satisfying $\beta + \gamma = 1$ or $\beta^2 + \beta\gamma + \gamma^2 = 0$. Consequently, for each of the $\frac{q - \sqrt{q} - 2}{2}$ pairs, $\alpha$ is uniquely determined. Thus, the total number of such characteristic polynomials is $\frac{q - \sqrt{q} - 2}{2}$.
